cal.q: Will one party to the conflict make a formal external response to a ceasefire plan within the seven-day window, thereby pushing the negotiations into a new stage?
Will there be public results within the seven-day window that show substantial agreement on key channel arrangements related to the ceasefire and significant convergence of differences?
Did the two parties carry out coordinated attacks on facilities close to key shipping lanes within the 7-day window and cause casualties?
Will the two parties publicly announce within the 7-day window that they will stop all attacks on shipping-related facilities?
Did the major countries outside the region jointly propose a multi-point plan to end the war within the 14-day window?
Will major countries outside the region publicly commit to using formal sanctions mechanisms to force all parties to accept the peace plan within the 14-day window?
Country Y Will the leader deliver a national address within the 14-day window and make directional statements that will intensify the crackdown within weeks?
Will the Country Y leader publicly announce an unconditional suspension of all military operations against Country X within the 14-day window?
Will Country Y and Country Z conduct joint air strikes on key energy-related industrial areas in Country X within a 30-day window?
Will Country X announce that its energy export capabilities have fully returned to pre-conflict levels within the 30-day window?

Has Country X publicly announced a directional threat to impose tougher restrictions or blockades on another important thoroughfare within the 30-day window?

Will there be a joint initiative promoted by major countries outside the region within the 30-day window, with the core demands of ceasefire and restoration of shipping lanes?
Will major countries outside the region publicly acknowledge within the 30-day window that their peace initiative has been officially signed and taken into effect by both parties to the conflict?
Is there a public escalation signal from Country Y from the highest level within the 14-day window that “the crackdown will be stepped up in the coming weeks”?

Does it appear within the 14-day window that Country Y has been publicly stated by the highest level that military operations will be strictly limited to domestic defense and that no force will be used externally?
Are there coordinated actions between Country Y and Country Z on Country X energy or export capacity-related goals within the 30-day window?
Will Country Y and Country Z publicly announce the cessation of coordinated actions and establish a joint cessation mechanism within the 30-day window?
Are there escalating threats via social media involving attacks on civilian infrastructure within the 30-day window, thereby increasing the risk of spillover?
Has Country Y made a public commitment within the 30-day window to avoid any involvement in civil infrastructure issues and to issue new binding rules to that effect?
Has the relevant parties publicly agreed within the 60-day window that the scope of the ceasefire is clear and there are no differences in interpretation?
Will new regulatory arrangements (such as tolls or permits) around key strait passages emerge within the 90-day window and spark controversy?
Will there be a definite conclusion within the 90-day window that passage through the key straits is publicly declared to be "completely free and no longer affected by any new regulations"?
Will the formal launch of coercive measures such as a naval blockade of the port of Country X occur within the 90-day window?
Is there a clear commitment from Country Y to publicly announce that no maritime restrictions will be imposed on Country X ports within the 90-day window?
Has a ceasefire window been announced or confirmed to have a clear start and end date within the 14-day window?
Is there a 14-day window in which a ceasefire is publicly announced to be terminated early and all-out airstrikes resumed?
Will the dispute over sea lane access rules shift from the military level to institutional arrangements (such as fees, permits) within the 30-day window?
Will there be a 30-day window for Country X to publicly withdraw its new arrangements for critical strait passage rules?
Is there an escalation of port-related operations from air strikes to maritime enforcement measures within the Country Y versus Country X 7-day window?
Will there be a 7-day window in which Country Y clearly announces that its maritime measures will restrict the passage of vessels from all countries equally?

Will there be a situation in which the advancement of negotiations and military operations occur in parallel within the 30-day window: while there is a ceasefire or progress in negotiations, there is a major strike or blockade on the other?
Will the overall conflict be downgraded to a state of mere verbal confrontations without any new military operations within the 30-day window?
Will there be an announcement within the 14-day window that Country X will temporarily impound some merchant ships passing through key straits to enforce the new regulations?
Will Country Y publicly announce the deployment of additional ground troops to the surrounding waters and the establishment of long-term garrison bases within the 14-day window?

Will Country Y announce its agreement to suspend airstrikes or strikes on Country X and set a clear ceasefire window?

As of about a week after the cutoff, has the mainstream of public opinion shifted to support the party that launched the strike and believe that its military actions are justified?

Within about two weeks after the major powers outside the region jointly proposed a ceasefire and war plan, has public opinion shifted towards strengthening multi-polar checks and balances and affirming the role of the mediating powers in promoting ceasefires and maintaining waterways?
After one side announces a two-week ceasefire window, will public opinion generally trust the sincerity of the ceasefire and become optimistic that the conflict will subside?

After the ceasefire was announced, there were repeated disputes over the scope of application (it did not restrict armed actions against third parties). About 18 days after the cutoff, is public opinion still skeptical and distrustful of whether the ceasefire can last?

After one party officially launches a naval blockade of its opponent's port, does public opinion generally accept that the blockade is legal and reasonable, and does not characterize it as a hegemonic or hooligan act?

Within 7 days of the cutoff, when the coalition forces attack Country X a dock adjacent to Strait A, causing casualties, will public opinion take on the tone of 'support Country X and oppose Country Y Country Z', sympathize with Country X, support its nuclear self-protection and reciprocal counterattack?

Within 14 days after the cutoff, public opinion will split into two groups: optimistic and pessimistic about the Strait A blockade - one group uses "Region L water" "Country W self-produced" and other jokes to relieve anxiety, while the other group is worried about the cost of spring plowing and food security?

Within 14 days of the cutoff, when the president of a certain country delivers a nationally televised speech on the conflict and threatens to "strike extremely hard" within two or three weeks, will public opinion ridicule him for "talking while bombarding" and compare Country Y to "Person B being beaten by Leader B"?

Within 30 days from the cutoff, will the mainstream of public opinion sympathize with Country X, support its tough counterattack, and condemn the air strikes on civilian facilities with collective indignation as 'too outrageous'?

Within 60 days from the cutoff, when a country threatens to blow up the Country X power plant and bridge, and Country X responds with a 'human chain' to protect the bridge, will public opinion compare the bridge protection to Country V's Anti-Japanese War, resonate with 'tears', and call Leader A 'the devil' and 'executioner'?

Within 30 days of the cutoff, when the president of a certain country suddenly agrees to a two-week ceasefire and oil prices plummet in response, will public opinion question the authenticity of the ceasefire, regard the 'ultimatum' as a strategic trap, and ridicule its 'Equipment A' for accidentally hitting the oil depot?

Within 90 days from the cutoff, when the blockade officially takes effect and thousands of ships and tens of thousands of seafarers are trapped, will public opinion strongly condemn the blockade as a "rogue act" and become deeply concerned about the safety of the trapped ships and seafarers?

Within 60 days after the cutoff, when the blockade of the Strait blocks global energy channels, will public opinion unanimously call on the country to remain neutral, avoid taking sides, and advocate not linking the blockade with its national destiny or institutional advantages?

Within 90 days after the cutoff, when the president of a certain country agrees to a two-week ceasefire, will public opinion unanimously praise him for showing a responsible statesman, believe that the ceasefire will be lasting, and be generally optimistic about the prospects for peace?

time.desc: One party to the conflict announced that it had submitted a formal reply to its opponent on a ceasefire plan containing multiple clauses. The ceasefire negotiations entered a new stage, but there are still major differences in key channel arrangements.
The two parties carried out joint attacks on Country X facilities close to key shipping channels and caused casualties, indicating that the war was still escalating in the context of negotiations.
Major countries outside the region have jointly proposed a multi-point peace plan to end the war. The core demands include an immediate ceasefire and the restoration of access to key waterways.
Country Y leaders address the nation, saying a tougher crackdown on Country X will be carried out within weeks and setting a time target for ending the conflict
Country Y and Country Z launched joint air strikes on Country X's important energy industrial park, directly attacking its energy and export capabilities.

Country Y leaders threatened on social platforms to bomb Country X civilian infrastructure and asked them to open the key strait, while Country X issued a counter-warning of possible escalation of blockade of another important channel.
Country Y announces agreement to suspend airstrikes and strikes on Country X and sets a two-week ceasefire window
Country Z made it clear that the ceasefire did not restrict its actions against relevant armed groups, triggering public disputes over the scope and sustainability of the ceasefire.
Country X Proposing tolls and other arrangements for passage in key straits has triggered legal disputes, highlighting the stalemate in negotiations on strait rules after the ceasefire

Country Y The military officially launched a naval blockade of the Country X port and stated that it would not affect the passage of ships in non-Country X ports, making the prospect of a ceasefire unclear again.

The leader of a major country publicly called on all countries to go to the key strait to compete for oil on their own, claiming that their opponents had been basically defeated, suggesting that they might loosen control of the strait, triggering a late-night surge in oil prices.

One side's navy began to mobilize troops to key straits to prepare for blockade of the opponent's ports. The relevant deployment was carried out simultaneously with the talks held by the two sides in a third country.
